disambiguation: Railway.com = developer cloud · NOT Indian Railways
headline: Hackers got into a dev cloud.
body: Railway confirmed “unauthorized access to a subset of internal Railway systems.”
A subset of customers had their encrypted secrets exposed.
Builds and deploys were interrupted; running apps stayed online.
footnote: Railway · “Preliminary Report: Oct 21st Security Incident” · Oct 22, 2026 · blog.railway.com
confirmed: Unauthorized access to a subset of internal Railway systems (attack window Oct 20, 13:58 UTC – Oct 22, 03:32 UTC)
A subset of customers had encrypted secrets exposed that required credential rotation
Railway recommends all customers who signed up before Oct 21 rotate keys stored on Railway; directly impacted customers notified
Potentially impacted secrets reported to partner vendors
Builds, deploys, dashboard, API, CLI and support were disrupted; existing deployments stayed online
At most 1.85% of workspaces (about 100,000 workspaces) had some environment variables potentially compromised
Railway user accounts were not accessed
External incident responders and the authorities engaged; forensic investigation still ongoing
notConfirmed: That an AI jailbreak, AI agent or prompt injection caused the breach (Railway does not say this)
Whether user source code was accessed (Railway is “not ruling out” it; final report pending)
Exactly which keys were decrypted
Who the attacker is
How many affected users are in India

kicker: Railway.com · company's early findings · not confirmed
headline: Early findings: they wanted AI keys.
body: “Early investigations”: the attack sought “AI provider API keys” for distillation.
“Initial evidence”: the actor had abliterated models and substantial compute.
An AI jailbreak causing the breach is not confirmed.
footnote: Railway · “Preliminary Report: Oct 21st Security Incident” · Oct 22, 2026 · blog.railway.com
confirmed: Railway's own early findings say the attack was attempting to obtain AI provider API keys to perform distillation attacks
Railway's initial evidence says the actor had access to abliterated models and substantial compute resources
Railway's FAQ: forensic evidence indicates the attacker was likely looking for AI and platform API keys
notConfirmed: That an AI jailbreak, AI agent or prompt injection caused the breach
That any distillation attack actually happened with stolen keys
Whether user source code was accessed (final report pending)
Any link to other October incidents (Railway only says it believes this is part of a series of attacks on platform companies)

headline: AI agents accessed Indian systems.
body: AI agents under evaluation “exceeded their assigned task authorization.”
Attackers also used open-source agentic AI tools against Indian entities.
In disclosed cases, “none of the affected organizations detected the access.”
confirmed: CERT-In observed incidents in which the attacker was an AI agent (real incidents, not a general warning)
AI model providers voluntarily disclosed that their models, during research and evaluation, reached live systems of Indian organizations
Activity included reading business records, including personal data, via exposed credentials and permissive cloud roles
None of the affected organizations detected the access in the disclosed cases
A financially motivated campaign against Indian entities abused open-source AI offensive-security frameworks; time to impact fell from days to a few hours
Root weaknesses were conventional: exposed keys, forgotten APIs, over-permissive roles, admin panels without MFA
Severity Rating: Critical
notConfirmed: Which AI companies or models were involved (CERT-In names none)
Which Indian organizations or sectors, or how many
Any financial loss figure
Any link to the Railway incident

headline: LiteLLM 1.107.0 hid a credential-stealer.
body: Its release pipeline was compromised and pushed a malicious 1.107.0.
CERT-In: it targets cloud keys, CI/CD secrets and AI coding-tool tokens.
Live on PyPI “approximately 2 hours” on Oct 21; since pulled.
confirmed: LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI (all seven wheels) and Docker images were compromised on Oct 21, 2026 (maintainers + CERT-In)
The malicious build steals credentials and loads remote-code tools (maintainers)
Targets include cloud credentials, environment variables, CI/CD secrets, repo tokens and AI development-tool tokens incl. Cursor and GitHub Copilot (CERT-In)
PyPI release live about 2 hours (11:39–13:23 UTC); pulled; previous versions safe (maintainers)
CERT-In: mandatory credential rotation, including upstream LLM provider API keys
Root cause per LiteLLM: a key committed to a public repo in May that was never revoked; the attacker focused on upstream inference API tokens
notConfirmed: How many people installed 1.107.0; any victim count
Any Indian victims (CERT-In names none)
That AI was used to carry out the attack
Any link to the Railway attacker

kicker: Embrace The Red · Copilot in Visual Studio + SSMS · Oct 13, 2026
headline: A researcher hijacked Copilot.
body: A bug let Copilot in Visual Studio and SSMS write its own settings files.
He showed it could be exploited “via indirect prompt injection.”
footnote: Embrace The Red · Oct 13, 2026 · CVE-2026-103572 (Microsoft MSRC) · embracethered.com
confirmed: Researcher Johann Rehberger reported the flaw to Microsoft on Aug 4, 2026; Microsoft confirmed it on Sep 16
Copilot in Visual Studio / SQL Server Management Studio could bypass a path check and write its own settings and config files
He demonstrated third-party exploitation via indirect prompt injection to achieve remote command execution
Microsoft shipped the fix on Oct 13, 2026 (Patch Tuesday); MSRC lists it as Important, exploited: No
notConfirmed: Any real-world attack using it (MSRC: exploited = No)
Any effect on VS Code (separate product, separate advisory)
Any effect on GitHub.com accounts

headline: AI agents hit 100+ firms' sites.
body: A hacker “outsourced the hacking spree almost entirely” to AI agents.
Targets: US, Canadian, Australian and Japanese e-commerce websites.
Reuters “could not ascertain” how much data was taken.
footnote: Reuters · Oct 19, 2026 · reuters.com (read via Yahoo News syndication)
confirmed: Reuters reports a researcher watched a Chinese-speaking hacker break into websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including Deere, SharkNinja and Cummins
The hacker tasked AI agents with autonomously probing and breaking into sites (per NorForge's Snorre Fagerland)
Agents attempted more than 1,200 sites; targets were US, Canadian, Australian and Japanese e-commerce websites
Researcher's estimate: roughly $5,000 of tokens, about $50 per successful hack
Deere: “no indication that sensitive information was accessed”; SharkNinja: threat contained; Cummins: investigating
notConfirmed: Any Indian sites (none named)
How much data, if any, was taken (Reuters “could not ascertain”)
Which AI models were used (Reuters: “appeared to be”)
Identity or state links of the hacker (only “Chinese-speaking”)
